# Incident Report: Vidar Infostealer Compromise

## 1. Scope of Evidence
- Source: `2022-01-07-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (5,880 packets, single host capture, 192.168.1.0/24 LAN)
- Capture window: 2022-01-07 20:04:09 → 20:16:40 (local capture clock), beginning at host boot (DHCP request) through Windows Update / AD housekeeping traffic. No separate IDS/Suricata export was present in the evidence directory — attribution below is **behavioral**, not signature-confirmed.

## 2. Victim Host
| Attribute | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | 192.168.1.216 | DHCP lease, all C2/AD traffic |
| MAC | 9c:5c:8e:32:58:f9 (ASUSTek Computer Inc.) | Frame 1 DHCP Request, ARP frames |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-GXMYNO2 | DHCP option 12, mDNS query `DESKTOP-GXMYNO2.local`, LLMNR query, Kerberos `CNameString` = `DESKTOP-GXMYNO2$` |
| AD domain | spoonwatch.net (NetBIOS: SPOONWATCH), DC = SPOONWATCH-DC (192.168.1.2) | DNS SRV lookups for `_ldap._tcp...spoonwatch.net`, NBNS registrations |
| Logged-in user | steve.smith | Kerberos AS-REQ/TGS-REQ `CNameString` = `steve.smith` (frames against DC 192.168.1.2) |

The delivery/initial-access vector is not visible in this capture — the capture starts at host boot, and the malicious session begins ~203 seconds later with no preceding DNS lookup or referring page, indicating the payload was already staged/executed on the host (or delivery occurred out-of-band before capture start).

## 3. Malware Family
**Vidar Stealer** (info-stealer), attribution level: **behavioral, not signature-confirmed** (no AV/IDS hits available in evidence).

Basis for the identification:
1. **Dependency-DLL staging pattern**: the bot pulled exactly seven files disguised as `.jpg` from a single C2 over one persistent HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connection. All seven are genuine PE32 DLLs, and their embedded import/version strings identify them as the legitimate Mozilla NSS / Visual C++ runtime libraries Vidar is known to fetch so it can open and decrypt Firefox/Chrome credential databases:
   - `1.jpg` → `sqlite3.dll` (645,592 bytes)
   - `2.jpg` → `freebl3.dll` / `nss3.dll` (334,288 bytes)
   - `3.jpg` → Mozilla NSS support DLL (137,168 bytes)
   - `4.jpg` → `msvcp140.dll` / `vcruntime140.dll` (440,120 bytes)
   - `5.jpg` → `nss3.dll` (1,246,160 bytes)
   - `6.jpg` → `freebl3.dll` / `softokn3.dll` / `nssdbm3.dll` (144,848 bytes)
   - `7.jpg` → `vcruntime140.dll` (83,784 bytes)
2. **C2 checkin/gate**: `POST /osk//main.php` immediately after the DLL set finished downloading (empty 200 ack).
3. **Exfiltration archive structure**: a single `POST /osk/` uploaded a 379,629-byte `multipart/form-data` body containing a ZIP named `_5861695120.zip` with the exact log layout Vidar produces per victim:
   - `autofill/Google Chrome_Default.txt`, `autofill/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`
   - `cc/Google Chrome_Default.txt`, `cc/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`
   - `cookies/Google Chrome_Network.txt`, `cookies/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`
   - `outlook.txt`, `passwords.txt`, `system.txt`, `screenshot.jpg`
4. **HTTP fingerprint on every request** (no `User-Agent`; `Accept-Language: ru-RU,ru;q=0.9,en;q=0.8`; `Accept-Charset: iso-8859-1, utf-8, utf-16, *;q=0.1`; `Cache-Control: no-cache`) — consistent across all nine requests to the C2, indicating a single hardcoded bot HTTP client rather than a browser.

## 4. Indicators of Compromise (all observed directly in the capture)

**C2 endpoint**
- `2.56.57.108:80` (TCP, HTTP/1.1, keep-alive) — no DNS lookup preceded this connection; the IP is hardcoded in the malware. No malicious domain was observed (only legitimate `*.microsoft.com`/`bing.com`/`msn.com` domains appear elsewhere in the capture, all benign Windows telemetry/update traffic).

**Malicious URLs (all `http://2.56.57.108`)**
| URL | Method | Direction | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/osk//6.jpg` | POST | download | 144,848 B (PE32 DLL) |
| `/osk//1.jpg` | POST | download | 645,592 B (PE32 DLL) |
| `/osk//2.jpg` | POST | download | 334,288 B (PE32 DLL) |
| `/osk//3.jpg` | POST | download | 137,168 B (PE32 DLL) |
| `/osk//4.jpg` | POST | download | 440,120 B (PE32 DLL) |
| `/osk//5.jpg` | POST | download | 1,246,160 B (PE32 DLL) |
| `/osk//7.jpg` | POST | download | 83,784 B (PE32 DLL) |
| `/osk//main.php` | POST | checkin | 200 empty ack |
| `/osk/` | POST | **exfiltration** | 379,629 B multipart upload |

**Transferred payload files & SHA-256 (response bodies, PE32 DLLs despite `.jpg` naming)**
| Served as | SHA-256 |
|---|---|
| `1.jpg` | `16574f51785b0e2fc29c2c61477eb47bb39f714829999511dc8952b43ab17660` |
| `2.jpg` | `a770ecba3b08bbabd0a567fc978e50615f8b346709f8eb3cfacf3faab24090ba` |
| `3.jpg` | `3fe6b1c54b8cf28f571e0c5d6636b4069a8ab00b4f11dd842cfec00691d0c9cd` |
| `4.jpg` | `334e69ac9367f708ce601a6f490ff227d6c20636da5222f148b25831d22e13d4` |
| `5.jpg` | `e2935b5b28550d47dc971f456d6961f20d1633b4892998750140e0eaa9ae9d78` |
| `6.jpg` | `43536adef2ddcc811c28d35fa6ce3031029a2424ad393989db36169ff2995083` |
| `7.jpg` | `c40bb03199a2054dabfc7a8e01d6098e91de7193619effbd0f142a7bf031c14d` |

**Exfiltrated data**
- Archive name (as sent in the multipart `Content-Disposition`): `_5861695120.zip`, uploaded to `POST /osk/` at 20:07 (per internal ZIP timestamps), total 379,629 bytes on the wire.
- SHA-256 of the ZIP payload extracted from the capture: `618cbd9e2554807aaa9a584219f261fbc835723664ad6f0130f0b141cfd75ffb`
- Contents confirm theft of: Chrome and Edge autofill data, Chrome and Edge saved payment-card data, Chrome and Edge cookies (Chrome cookies file alone 137,885 bytes), Outlook data (`outlook.txt`), saved passwords (`passwords.txt`), a desktop screenshot (`screenshot.jpg`, 271,977 bytes), and host system info (`system.txt`) — all from host DESKTOP-GXMYNO2, user steve.smith.

## 5. Non-malicious traffic (ruled out)
All other TLS/HTTP activity in the capture (`v10/v20.events.data.microsoft.com`, `settings-win.data.microsoft.com`, `www.bing.com`, `api.msn.com`, `client.wns.windows.com`, `download.windowsupdate.com`, `ctldl.windowsupdate.com`, Delivery Optimization peers) is standard Windows 10/11 telemetry, Defender definition updates, and Windows Update, all resolved via legitimate Microsoft DNS records and destined for Microsoft-owned IP space. AD traffic (LDAP, Kerberos, SMB/DCE-RPC, CLDAP, NetLogon to 192.168.1.2 `SPOONWATCH-DC`) reflects normal domain-joined logon/authentication, not malicious lateral movement.

## 6. Recommended Actions
- Isolate 192.168.1.216 from the network immediately; treat all credentials cached or used by `steve.smith` on this host as compromised (domain password, browser-saved passwords, cookies, Outlook credentials, card data).
- Force a domain password reset for `steve.smith` and invalidate any active sessions/cookies tied to accounts stored in Chrome/Edge on this host.
- Block/alert on `2.56.57.108:80` and the URI pattern `/osk/*.jpg` + `/osk/main.php` at the perimeter and EDR.
- Image and forensically preserve DESKTOP-GXMYNO2 before remediation; reimage before returning to service.
